1.19.m: Bhīṣma said: / The highest glorification of Puṣkara and of Nandā has been heard, / when a crore of ṛṣis came to Puṣkara from seeing the face [of Brahmā].
Supreme beauty was obtained by all; all this has been heard by me. / Those [places] that were measured out with sacrificial cords, tell me about them:
How was the division of sacred places made by those great-souled ones? / And the sacred places made by the great sages at the hermitage,
the footprint formerly made by Viṣṇu on the Mountain of Sacrifice, / and the five sacred places made there by those deadly poisonous serpents,
and the step-well for offering rice-balls—by whom was it made formerly? / And how did the Sarasvatī, the Gaṅgā, go into the ground facing north?
How should a pilgrimage to the three Puṣkaras be undertaken by brāhmaṇas who know the Vedas? / What fruit arises from it—tell me that.
Pulastya said: / This great burden of questions has been arranged by you; / therefore, with a one-pointed mind, hear the great fruit of the sacred place.
He whose hands, feet, and mind are well restrained, / and [who possesses] learning, austerity, and renown, enjoys the fruit of a sacred place.
He who turns away from accepting gifts, is content with whatever comes, / and is free from egotism, enjoys the fruit of a sacred place.

He who is free from anger, O king of kings, whose nature is truth, whose vows are firm,
and who regards all beings as himself, enjoys the fruit of tirthas.
This is the supreme secret of the sages, O best of the Bharatas, / where formerly, O great king, at the sacrificial session of the Grandfather,
a crore of ascetics of fierce austerities arrived; / relying on the sight of his face, they remained at Jyeṣṭhapuṣkara.
Having obtained supreme handsome form, those best of sages were pleased; / filled with great joy, they were eager for the sight of Brahmā.
Having measured the ground in all four directions with their sacrificial cords, / and having made the sacred place and the division, they remained devoted to worship.
And then the Grandfather, drawing near them, was pleased; / seeing that crore of wise ones, and seeing their measurement, [he said]:
'From this day forward, the increase of dharma will belong to you; / whatever mortal, having come here, will first immerse whatever limb in the water,
for the sake of beauty, beautiful form will be produced by the sacred place; / there is no doubt, within a circle extending a yojana.
Half a yojana in width and one and a half yojanas in length: / this is the measure of the sacred place established by the crore of ṛṣis.
Just by going to Puṣkara, O king of kings, O subduer of enemies, / a mortal obtains the fruit of both the Rājasūya and the horse sacrifice.
The most sacred Sarasvatī entered into Jyeṣṭhapuṣkara; / there, the gods headed by Brahmā, sages, siddhas, and cāraṇas
assemble, O king of kings, on the fourteenth day of the bright half of Caitra; / devoted to the worship of ancestors and gods, one should perform a bath there.'

Then one obtains [the merit of] a cow sacrifice and raises up his family.
Thus was the division of sacred places made by those great sages.

Having satisfied the ancestors and the gods, one is honored in the world of Viṣṇu.
Having bathed there, a mortal becomes stainless like the moon.

He attains the world of Brahmā and goes to the supreme state.
In the world of mortals, the sacred place of the god of gods, renowned throughout the three worlds,

famous by the name Puṣkara, is the destroyer of great sins.
Indeed, a hundred million sacred places, O ruler of the earth,

are present at Puṣkara at the three junctions of the day, O delight of your family.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, together with the hosts of Maruts,

and Gandharvas and Apsarases are constantly present there, O mighty one,
where gods, Daityas, and Brahmarṣis, having performed austerities,

endowed with divine yoga and great merit, [dwell], O great king.
Even for the wise man who merely desires in his mind to go to the Puṣkaras,

all sins are purified, and he rejoices upon the vault of heaven.
In that sacred place, O great king, the Grandfather [Brahmā] constantly

dwelt with supreme delight, esteemed by gods and Dānavas.
At the Puṣkaras, O great king, the gods, preceded by the sages,

attained perfection, endowed with great merit.
Whoever performs an ablution there, devoted to worshipping the ancestors and the gods,

the wise declare [the fruit to be] ten times greater than a horse sacrifice.
Even if one feeds a single brāhmaṇa while resorting to the forest of Puṣkara,

ten million are satisfied and worshipped with that food.
By that deed, O Bhīṣma, he rejoices here and in the hereafter.

With herbs, roots, or fruits, or with whatever he supports himself,
he should give that indeed to a brāhmaṇa, full of faith and free from malice.

By that alone, a wise man would obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Whether a brāhmaṇa, a kṣatriya, a vaiśya, or a śūdra, O best of kings,

the holy lake of the Grandfather is renowned by the name Puṣkara,
which indeed bestows merit upon Vaikhānasa ascetics, perfected ones, and sages,

from where the most holy Sarasvatī goes to the great ocean,
where the primeval god, the great yogin Madhusūdana, dwells,

celebrated by the name Ādivarāha, worshipped by the thirty [gods].
And those castes that are of low caste who go to the sacred place of the Grandfather,

having bathed in the sacred place of the great-souled one, do not go to a lower birth.
And especially he who goes to Puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārttika—

imperishable is his fruit there: so have we heard.
Moreover, whoever remembers the Puṣkaras evening and morning with folded hands,

by him ablution has been performed in every sacred place, O descendant of Kuru.
Whatever sin has been committed from birth, by a woman or by a man,

all that is destroyed merely by bathing at Puṣkara.
Just as the Grandfather is the foremost of all the gods,

even so the sacred place Puṣkara is said to be the foremost of sacred places.
Having seen it, being restrained and pure at Puṣkara for ten years,

he attains all sacrifices and goes to the world of Brahmā.
Whereas one attends upon the agnihotra for a full hundred years,

or dwells for a single Kārttikī at Puṣkara, the two are indeed equal.
At Puṣkara an oblation is hard to perform; at Puṣkara austerity is hard to perform;

at Puṣkara giving is hard to do; and residence is exceedingly hard to maintain.
A brāhmaṇa who knows the Veda, having gone to Jyeṣṭhapuṣkara,

becomes a recipient of liberation through bathing, and through a śrāddha a deliverer of his ancestors.
Even a brāhmaṇa by mere name who goes and performs the twilight worship

has indeed performed the twilight worship for twelve years here,
without a doubt; this was spoken of old by the Self-born [Brahmā].

The fault described in the Sāvitrī does not arise in his family.
Whatever wife gives water with a copper vessel to her husband

who is about to perform the twilight worship, having been liberated, goes to heaven;
having reached the world of Brahmā, she remains for a day of Brahmā.

Even if one has gone alone, the twilight devotion should be venerated in due order
with water of Puṣkara kept in a pitcher;

by that too, twilight worship has been performed for twelve years, there is no doubt.
If the wife is standing near him while he performs the libation to the ancestors,

facing the southern direction with the Gāyatrī, O best of kings,
supreme satisfaction lasting for twelve years is made for the ancestors;

by the funeral ball [satisfaction] for a thousand yugas [is attained], and by the śrāddha he obtains endless [fruit].
It is for this purpose that the wise take wives:

"Having gone to a sacred place, we will offer funeral balls preceded by a śrāddha."
For them, sons, wealth, grain, and an unbroken lineage

will surely come to pass, there is no doubt; this the Grandfather declared.
Having satisfied the ancestors and the gods, one obtains the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma.

I shall also tell you of the hermitages; listen with single-minded attention, O king.
Here an ashram equal to the gods was established by Agastya;

here of old was the ashram of the Seven Sages, esteemed by the gods,
and here is the supreme ashram of the Brahmarṣis and of the Manus,

and the delightful city of the Nāgas on the bank of the Yajñaparvata.
The power of Agastya of immeasurable soul, O great king,

I tell you in brief; listen with utmost concentration.
Formerly in the Kṛta age, O Bhīṣma, there were Dānavas arrogant in battle,

known as the Kāleyas, hosts of exceedingly fierce ones.
Relying on Vṛtra, they were intent upon destroying the gods.

Then the terrified gods approached Brahmā.
To all of them who stood with folded hands, the Supreme Lord spoke:

"All that you wish to accomplish is known to me, O gods.
I shall tell you that means by which you will slay Vṛtra.

There is a great sage of noble intellect, famous as Dadhīci.
All of you together go to him and ask for a boon.

He, the righteous-souled one, will give it to you with an inner self well pleased.
He should be addressed by all of you together, desiring victory:

'Grant your own bones out of a desire for the welfare of the three worlds.'
Casting off his body, he will give his own bones.

From his bones let a most terrible, firm thunderbolt be fashioned,
a great enemy-slaying divine weapon, known as the thunderbolt.

With that thunderbolt Śatakratu [Indra] will surely slay Vṛtra.
All this has been explained to you; therefore let it all be carried out."

Being spoken to thus, the gods, having taken leave of the Grandfather
and placing Śatakratu at their head, went to Dadhīci's ashram

on the farther shore of the Sarasvatī, filled with various trees and creepers,
resounding with the hum of singing bees, like Sāman-singers,

interspersed with the calls of male cuckoos, made resonant by jīvañjīvaka birds,
with buffaloes, boars, sṛmaras, and yaks

wandering here and there, devoid of fear of tigers,
and with female and male elephants with temples cleft by rutting,

sporting with outpourings of sound, made to echo all around,
resounding with lions and tigers roaring with a great roar,

and with hidden peacocks dwelling in caves and clefts;
and made delightful to the mind, resounding in various bowers—

they arrived at Dadhīci's ashram, which was comparable to heaven.
There they saw that Dadhīci, radiant as the sun.

blazing with his body just as the four-armed [Viṣṇu does] with Lakṣmī.
O king, all the gods, having greeted and bowed down at his feet,
begged for the boon as had been stated by Parameṣṭhin.

Then Dadhīci, extremely delighted, spoke this to those foremost among the gods:
“I shall do today what is for your benefit, O gods, and I abandon my own body.”

Having thus spoken to them, that best of bipeds at once cast off his life-breaths;
and the gods, together with Indra, took his bones as needed.

Rejoicing in form, the gods approached Tvaṣṭṛ for the sake of victory and explained the matter to him.
And Tvaṣṭṛ, having heard their words, joyful in form, restrained and with great effort,

made a thunderbolt of exceedingly terrible power; and having crafted the weapon, he spoke gladly to him:
“With this most excellent weapon, O god, reduce to ashes today the fierce enemy of the gods,

and then, having slain the foe along with his host, rule happily over the whole of heaven, dwelling in heaven.”
Thus addressed by Tvaṣṭṛ, Puraṃdara, overjoyed, attentively took hold of the thunderbolt.

Then, endowed with the thunderbolt and worshipped by the deities,
he approached Vṛtra, who stood enveloping heaven and earth,

protected on all sides by the gigantic Kālakeyas
with their weapons raised, like mountains with their peaks.

Then a battle took place between the gods and the Dānavas,
O best of the Bharatas, lasting for a moment, terrifying to the world and great.

By swords raised and hurled by heroes' arms,
and by bodies torn apart, there arose a tremendous noise.

And with heads falling down from the sky to the surface of the earth,
O protector of the earth, it appeared covered by them like palm trees.

Wearing golden armor, with iron clubs as weapons, the Kāleyas
charged against the gods like trees consumed by a forest fire.

The gods, united, were unable to withstand the speed of those rushing forward with great force;
broken, they fled out of fear.

Seeing them fleeing in terror, and Vṛtra growing in size,
great despondency entered the thousand-eyed Puraṃdara.

Seeing Śakra overcome by despondency, eternal Viṣṇu
infused his own splendor into Śakra, increasing his strength.

Seeing Śakra nourished by Viṣṇu, all the hosts of gods
then added their splendor, as did the stainless Brahmarṣis.

Nourished by Viṣṇu together with the deities
and the blessed Ṛṣis, Śakra became powerful.

Knowing that the lord of the gods had regained his strength, Vṛtra roared a tremendous roar.
By his roar, the earth, the directions, the sky, the heavens, and the mountains—all trembled.

Then Mahendra, exceedingly agitated on hearing that most terrible, great roar,
sunk in fear, swiftly hurled the great thunderbolt upon his head.

Struck by Śakra's thunderbolt, he fell with a great sound, wearing a golden garland,
like the excellent great Mandara mountain hurled formerly from Viṣṇu's hand.

When that foremost of Daityas was slain, Śakra, tormented by fear, fled to enter a lake;
he thought the thunderbolt had slipped from his hand, and from fear did not even see that Vṛtra was slain.

All the gods, joyful and delighted, and the sages then praised him;
and having quickly assembled, the gods struck down the remaining Daityas, tormented by Vṛtra's death.

Being slaughtered then by the gods, the great Asuras, swift as the wind,
entered the ocean out of fear; and having entered the immeasurable sea,

abounding in fish and full of jewels, they then held counsel together.
There, certain among them who knew how to resolve their thoughts, reflecting upon various strategies,

oppressed by fear and tormented by the host of gods, resolved upon the destruction of the three worlds.
Then, due to the impending time of their destruction, a terrible resolve arose in them as they deliberated:

“Those who are endowed with knowledge and ascetic power—their destruction must be accomplished first.
For all the worlds are upheld by ascetic power; therefore, make haste to destroy ascetic power.

Whoever there are on earth who are ascetics, knowers of dharma, and conversant with that—
let them be slain quickly; once they are gone, the world is ruined.”

Thus, all of them, having settled their minds and rejoicing exceedingly in the destruction of the world,
took refuge in the ocean, Varuṇa's inaccessible abode filled with great waves and treasures.

Having reached the ocean, Varuṇa's domain, the receptacle of waters,
the Kāleyas applied themselves to the destruction of the three worlds.

At night, thoroughly enraged, they devoured the sages
who were in hermitages and sacred sanctuaries.

In Vasiṣṭha's hermitage, one hundred and eighty-eight Brahmins
were eaten by those evil-minded ones, and other ascetics in the forest.

Having gone to Cyavana's holy hermitage frequented by twice-born,
a hundred sages who lived on fruits and roots were devoured.

Thus acting by night, they entered the ocean by day.
Going to Bharadvāja's hermitage, restrained celibate students,

subsisting on air and consuming water, twenty in number, were slaughtered.
Thus in turn, for the sake of devouring the sages, the Dānavas then

roamed about in the night, capable through the strength of their arms;
over a long time they indeed killed many hosts of sages.

And human beings did not notice them, O ruler of men,
as the world became devoid of recitation of the Veda and the vaṣaṭ-call, with its sacrificial and festive rites lost.

The world became dispirited, afflicted by the fear of the Kāleyas.
Thus being decimated, O lord of men, those human beings,

intent on saving themselves, fled in fear in the ten directions.
Some entered caves, and other twice-born were scattered.

Others, agitated by terror, abandoned their lives out of fear.
Some great archers there, brave and exceedingly proud,

made the greatest effort, searching for the Dānavas,
but they could not pursue them, who had taken refuge in the ocean.

They found no peace, and the world only met with destruction;
when the world was brought to ruin, its sacrificial and festive rites vanished,

the gods came together, exceedingly troubled, O lord of men,
and meeting with Mahendra, they held counsel out of fear.

Placing Nārāyaṇa, the invincible Vaikuṇṭha, at their head,
those assembled gods then spoke to Madhusūdana:

“You are our creator, protector, and the maintainer of the world, O Lord.
By you this entire world was created, both what moves and what does not move.

By you formerly the earth, lost in the ocean, O lotus-eyed one,
was lifted up for the sake of the world, assuming the boar form.

The primal Daitya of great prowess, Hiraṇyakaśipu, formerly,
was slain by you having assumed a man-lion form, O Puruṣottama.

And the great Asura Bali, who could not be slain by any beings,
was cast down by you from the three worlds, assuming a dwarf form.

The Asura famous as Jambha, a very great archer
who caused disturbance to sacrifices and was cruel, was cast down by you among the gods.

Such and other deeds, of which there is no counting, [are yours].
Of us who are terrified by fear, you are the refuge, O Madhusūdana.”
Therefore, O God of gods, for the sake of the worlds we inform you: / protect the worlds, the gods, and Indra from this great danger.

"By your grace, all four kinds of living beings continue to exist;
mortals become healthy, and the sky-dwellers [are nourished] by offerings to the gods and ancestors."
For the worlds proceed in this way, mutually supporting one another, / free from anxiety by your power, protected by you alone.
And now this supreme fear has come upon the worlds, / and we do not know by whom these brāhmaṇas are being slain at night.
And when the brāhmaṇas are destroyed, the earth will meet destruction. / By your grace, O mighty-armed Lord of the universe, may all the worlds
not meet destruction, being guarded indeed by you.” / Viṣṇu said: / “O gods, the entire cause of the destruction of creatures is known to me.
I shall also tell it to you; listen, free from distress! / There are extremely fierce hordes known as the Kālakeyas.
Seeing Vṛtra slain by the wise Thousand-eyed One [Indra], / they entered the abode of Varuṇa, protecting their lives.
Having entered the terrible ocean filled with various sea-monsters, / they slay the sages here at night to destroy the world.
Yet they cannot be brought to destruction, concealed as they are inside the ocean. / Let a plan be considered by you for the destruction of the ocean.”
Hearing these words spoken by Viṣṇu, / the gods approached Parameṣṭhin [Brahmā] and went to Agastya's hermitage.
There they saw the great-souled son of Varuṇa, blazing with brilliance, / attended upon by ṛṣis, as the Grandfather [Brahmā] is by the gods.
Approaching the high-souled son of Mitra and Varuṇa, the best, / vigilant, an abyss of austerities, attended by his own fulfilled rites,
the gods said: / “Formerly, you were the refuge of the worlds afflicted by Nahuṣa, / and that thorn of the world was brought down from the sovereignty of the gods for the sake of the world.
Growing great out of anger towards the Sun, the best of mountains, / Mount Vindhya, does not grow, not disobeying your command.
When the world was veiled in darkness and the creatures were oppressed by death, / they reached supreme relief having come to you alone as their protector.
You are indeed the constant refuge for us, who are terrified with fear. / Therefore today we beg a boon of you, for you are a granter of boons.”
Bhīṣma said: / “Why did the Vindhya suddenly grow, overcome with anger? / I wish to hear this in detail, O great sage.”
Pulastya said: / “At rising and setting, the Sun used to circumambulate / the king of mountains, the great mount Meru, the golden mountain.
Seeing him then, the Vindhya mountain spoke to the Sun: / ‘Just as Meru is constantly encircled by you
and circumambulated, do so for me, O Sun!’ / Addressed in this way, the Sun then answered the king of mountains:
‘I do not circumambulate this mountain out of my own desire; / this path has been assigned to me by the one by whom this world was created.’
Spoken to thus, the mountain then suddenly grew out of anger, / wishing to block the path of the sun and the moon, O scorcher of foes.
Then all the gods together with Indra, having assembled, / restrained the great king of mountains rising up, but he did not heed their words.
Then indeed they went to the sage residing in his hermitage, the best of ascetic and righteous men, / to Agastya of wondrous and blazing prowess; and those gods together addressed that noble one:
The gods said: / ‘This Vindhya, king of mountains, following the sway of anger, / blocks the path of the sun and moon and the course of the constellations.
No one else is able to restrain him, O lord of sages!’ / Hearing those words of the gods, the brāhmaṇa went to the mountain.
Having approached, he spoke to the Vindhya standing respectfully before him: / ‘I desire a path given by you, O best of mountains.
I am going to the southern quarter on a certain task; / until my return, wait for me!
When I have returned, O lord of mountains, then grow according to your desire!’” / Pulastya said: / “Even today, the son of Varuṇa has not returned from the southern region.
This all has been told to you, how the Vindhya does not grow / through the power of Agastya, which you asked me about.
Now hear from me as I relate how the Kāleyas / were slain by all the gods through the means of Agastya, O king.
Hearing the words of the thirty [gods], the son of Mitra and Varuṇa said: / ‘For what purpose have you come? What boon do you desire from me?’
Addressed thus by him then, the gods said to that sage: / ‘We desire one wondrous boon: drink the ocean, O divine sage, O great-souled one!
We wish the great ocean to be drunk up entirely when this is done by you, O great sage; / then we shall strike down, along with its followers, the army of the enemies of the gods named Kāleyas.’
Hearing the words of the thirty [gods], the sage said, ‘So be it! / I shall accomplish your wish, which brings happiness to the worlds.’
Having spoken thus, he then went to the ocean, the reservoir of waters, / together with the sages perfected by austerities and the gods, O you of good vows.
Humans, serpents, gandharvas, yakṣas, and kimpuruṣas likewise / followed the great-souled one, wishing to witness that wonder.
Then, together, he beheld the ocean roaring terribly, / as though dancing with its waves, as though bounding with the wind,
as though laughing with masses of foam, and crashing into caverns, / crowded with various aquatic monsters, and filled with various flocks of birds.
The gods together with Agastya, along with the gandharvas and great serpents, / and the fortunate ṛṣis approached the great ocean.
Having approached the ocean, the blessed ṛṣi, son of Varuṇa, / spoke to the assembled gods and those gathered ṛṣis,
Agastya, the best of ṛṣis, wishing to drink up the ocean: / ‘For the welfare of the world, I am drinking the abode of Varuṇa.
Whatever is to be performed by you, let that quickly be arranged!’ / Having spoken this word in their presence, the son of Mitra and Varuṇa,
enraged, drank the ocean while all the world looked on. / And seeing the ocean being drunk, the gods together with Indra
experienced supreme amazement and worshipped [him] with praises: / ‘You are our protector and creator, the creator of the worlds! / By your grace, the entire world shall regain its level state.’
Being worshipped by the thirty [gods], as the chiefs of the gandharvas sang, / and being showered with heavenly flowers, the great-souled one made the great ocean devoid of water.
Seeing the great ocean made devoid of water, all the gods, exceedingly delighted, / seized their excellent divine weapons and struck those Dānavas, undaunted in spirit.
Being slain by the great-souled, exceedingly powerful, roaring gods rushing with speed, / they could not withstand the onset of those swift and great-souled dwellers of heaven.
Being slain by the thirty [gods], those Dānavas of terrible roaring / fought a very tumultuous battle for about a moment, O Bhārata.
They had previously been burned by the ascetic heat of the sages whose minds were purified; / though striving with all their might, they were utterly destroyed by the thirty [gods].
Adorned with golden necklets, wearing earrings and armlets, / they lay slain, shining splendidly like flowering kiṃśuka trees.
Then some surviving best of the Kāleya Danavas, / cleaving the divine earth, took refuge in the depths of Pātāla.
Seeing the Dānavas slain, the gods praised the foremost of sages / with diverse words, and spoke this utterance:
“By your grace, O fortunate one, great joy has been attained by the worlds, / and by your radiance the Kāleyas of terrible valour have been slain.
Fill up the ocean again, O great Brahmin, the source of well-being for the worlds; / release back into it the water that you drank.”
Addressed thus, the blessed foremost of sages replied: / “That water has indeed been digested by me; let another expedient be devised
by you making an effort to fill the ocean.” / Hearing that speech of the great sage of perfected mind,
the gods together became amazed and despondent. / Taking leave of one another and bowing to the foremost of sages,
all the creatures, O great king, and the Brahmins went as they had come. / The gods, along with Viṣṇu, went to the Grandfather,
deliberating among themselves about filling the ocean. / With palms joined in reverence, all spoke concerning the filling of the ocean.
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, said to them who had assembled: / “Go, all you gods, as you please and according to your wish.
After a great lapse of time the ocean will return to its natural state. / Making his kinsmen the cause, the great king Bhagīratha
will fill the ocean again with the flood of the Gaṅgā.” / Having thus dispatched the gods, O best of sages, Brahmā,
the blessed one, being pleased, spoke to Agastya, the best of sages: / “The task of the gods, the destruction of the Dānavas, has indeed been performed by you.
Since the gods were rescued [by you], I am truly pleased with you, O sage; / ask for whatever boon you desire, and I will grant it.”
Thus addressed, Agastya then, after bowing down, [said]: / “Remaining here, O god, this task of the gods was accomplished by me.
Let this hermitage of mine become the foremost of all hermitages; / and as it is spoken by you, O blessed one, so it will be, no doubt.”
Brahmā said: / “Those men who, having made a pilgrimage to Puṣkara, come here, / and who bathe here in the pools and offer libations to the ancestors and gods,
and worship the gods—all that will produce inexhaustible [merit]. / Offering various kinds of water, and then sweetmeats and cakes
they will give to the foremost of the twice-born, their residence will be in heaven. / The ancestors will be satisfied by their ancestral rite until the cosmic dissolution.
And whoever satisfies a sage with roots and fruits, / having reached the realm of the Seven Sages, rejoices for eternal years.
Having climbed the sacrificial mountain and seen the outflow of the Gaṅgā, / the divine river flowing northward towards Puṣkara,
whoever performs a ritual bath here, intent on worshipping the ancestors and gods, / certainly obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice; there is no doubt.
And whoever feeds one Brahmin feeds ten million; / food and drink given here, O lord of sages, is inexhaustible.
Whatever wish one desires, all that will be his; / having merely bathed here, a human being does not go to a non-human birth on earth.
The highest of places, the best of sacred sites— / this has been granted by me, O best of sages; it will be so, no doubt.
Whatever sin has been committed from birth onward by a woman or a man, / by merely bathing right here, all of it is destroyed.”
Having spoken thus, the blessed Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, / bid farewell to the sage, the best of sages, Agastya, and departed.
Agastya also remained there in his hermitage, O scorcher of foes. / This origin of Agastya's hermitage has been recounted to you.
I shall also tell of the hermitages of the Seven Sages, O bearer of the Kuru line: / Atri, and Vasiṣṭha, then Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Aṅgiras, and Gautama, Sumati, likewise Sumukha, / Viśvāmitra, Sthūlaśiras, Saṃvarta, and Pratardana,
Raibhya, and Bṛhaspati, Cyavana, Kaśyapa, Bhṛgu, / Durvāsas, Jamadagni, and Mārkaṇḍeya, then Gālava,
Uśanas, then Bharadvāja, likewise the sage Yavakrīta, / Sthūlākṣa, Sakalākṣa, Kaṇva, Medhātithi, Kṛta,
Nārada, and Parvata, the twice-born Svagandhicyavana, / Tṛṇāmbuśabala, Dhaumya, Śatānanda, Kṛtavraṇa,
Jamadagni, likewise Rāma, and Aṣṭaka, and others, / and Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana accompanied by his sons and disciples—
these, having reached Puṣkara, in the hermitage of the Seven Sages, / were bound by observances and endowed with compassion, ascetic practitioners.
Harmlessness, restraint, fortitude, austerity, truth, patience, uprightness, / compassion, generosity, and repetition of mantras were established in all of them.
Whatever action is performed here is experienced in the other world; / knowing it to be thus, the sages were devoted to the ultimate truth.
Atheists do not go there, nor thieves, nor those whose senses are uncontrolled, / nor the cruel, nor slanderers, nor the ungrateful, nor the arrogant.
Truthful, radiant, heroic, compassionate, devoted to patience, / sacrificers and regular in sacrifice, desireless, free from distress,
free from possessiveness, free from egotism—such go there to Puṣkara. / Disease, old age, and death will not belong to the great-souled ones there.
Fools do not enter there, men devoted to sense objects, / afflicted by desire, greed, pride, malice, anger, and delusion.
Alike in honour and dishonour, free from dualities, with controlled senses, / and devoted to the yoga of meditation—they indeed go to Puṣkara.
The twice-born who abide properly in the hermitages as prescribed, / to protect the restraint [of passions]—theirs are the worlds of great fortune.
Those who do not harm living beings by action, thought, or word, / who are exceedingly gentle, virtuous, and always speaking pleasantly,
always devoted to the fire sacrifice, always honouring guests, / always possessing Vedic study, and always intent on bathing,
who look upon other men's wives as a mother, as a sister, / and also as a daughter, ever free from desire,
who do not become angry when reviled, and do not harm when harmed, / the great-souled ones, equanimous in pain and pleasure, with senses controlled—
all of them indeed perceiving [this], wandered this earth in ancient times, / contemplating the eternal world of Brahmā through absorption.
Then once there occurred a great drought; / practically the entire world was in severe distress, afflicted with hunger.
Then, in this world devoid of grain, seeking to protect themselves, / in extreme distress they took a dead boy and cooked [him].
Then the king, wandering about there and seeing the sages suffering, / stricken with grief, spoke this speech at that time:
The king said: / “Acceptance of gifts is seen as an unblamable livelihood for Brahmins; / therefore, accept gifts from me, O best of sages—
excellent villages, rice, barley, liquids, jewels, gold, / cows, and milch-cows—all that; do not cook meat, O twice-born!”
The sages said: / “O king, acceptance of gifts is terrible, tasting like honey but resembling poison; / why do you entice us who know that?
An oil-presser is equal to ten slaughter-houses; an owner of a flag is equal to ten oil-pressers; / a prostitute is equal to ten owners of flags; a king is equal to ten prostitutes.
A vintner runs ten thousand slaughter-houses; / a king is equal to him, and acceptance of his gifts is terrible.”

The brāhmaṇa who accepts [gifts] from a king, deluded by greed,
is cooked in dreadful hells such as Tāmisra.

"Therefore go, may you have well-being together with [your] gift, O king; / let this be given to others." Having said this, they departed for the forest.

Then, by the king's command, the ministers went there
and scattered cluster figs containing gold on the surface of the earth.

Then, searching for food, they picked up the cluster figs;
knowing they were heavy, Atri said they should not be accepted.

Atri said:
'We are not of foolish discernment; we are not of dull wit.
We know these are filled with gold; we are awakened, possessing knowledge.

This wealth brings pleasure only here in this world; its fruit in the hereafter is obstructed.
Therefore, it must never be taken by one who desires unending happiness.

And he who would accept from another a gold coin multiplied by a hundred,
accompanied by a thousand, attains the most sinful destination.

Whatever rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women exist on earth
is indeed not enough for a single person—considering this, one should attain calm.'

Vasiṣṭha said:
'He who has an accumulation of austerities and he who has an accumulation of possessions—
an accumulation of austerities alone is superior in this world to an accumulation of wealth.

For one who abandons all accumulations, troubles perish;
indeed, no one possessed of an accumulation is seen to be free from trouble.

The more a brāhmaṇa refuses to accept an improper gift,
the more his brāhmanical splendour increases through contentment.

He weighed poverty and kingship equally upon a balance;
for one who has restrained himself, poverty was greater even than kingship.'

Kaśyapa said:
'This is ruin for a brāhmaṇa, namely, a great hoard of wealth.

For a twice-born, bewildered by wealth and lordship, falls from the highest good;
an abundance of wealth leads to delusion, and delusion leads to hell.

Therefore, one who seeks the highest good should abandon from afar wealth, which is called ruin.
For one whose exertion for wealth is for the sake of dharma, non-exertion is better.

For rather than washing off mud, it is better not to touch it from afar.
Dharma that is accomplished through wealth is declared to be perishable;

hope for wealth and hope for life do not age, even as he ages.
The eyes and ears age; thirst alone remains unaffected.

Just as a tailor guides the thread into cloth with a needle,
even so the thread of saṃsāra is guided by the needle of thirst.

Just as the horn of a deer grows as its body grows,
so thirst—boundless, insatiable, bringing hundreds of miseries,

and full of adharma—grows; therefore, one should abandon it.'
Gautama said:
'Who, being contented, cannot sustain his life even on fruits?

Through greediness of the senses, a man plunges into straits;
for him whose mind is contented, prosperity is everywhere.

For one whose feet are covered with sandals, the earth is, as it were, covered with leather.
The bliss of those of calmed minds who are satiated with the nectar of contentment—

whence could that come to those greedy for wealth, running hither and thither?
Discontent is the ultimate misery; contentment is the supreme bliss.

Therefore, a person desiring happiness should be constantly contented.'
Viśvāmitra said:
'If a desire is fulfilled for someone who desires,

then another desire pierces him again like an arrow.
Never is desire extinguished by the enjoyment of desires;

it only increases all the more, like fire fed with ghee.
Yearning for desires through delusion, a man does not grow in happiness,

just like a francolin going into the shade of a tree that is the home of a hawk.
He who enjoys this earth up to the borders of the four oceans,

and he for whom a stone and gold are equal—the latter has accomplished his purpose, not the king.'
Jamadagni said:
'He who does not take an acceptance, even though capable of acceptance,

attains the eternal worlds belonging to the virtuous who are devoted to giving.
A vipra who would desire wealth from a king is to be grieved by great sages;

that foolish-minded man does not see the fear of torment in hell.
Even though capable of acceptance, one should not become attached to acceptance;

the brāhmanical splendour of vipras is extinguished by acceptance.
For those capable of acceptance who turn away from acceptance,

the very worlds that belong to givers belong also to those who do not accept.'
Arundhatī said:
'Just as the lotus fibre, remaining in water, would always enter constantly,

so also thirst, without beginning or end, is ever located in the body.
For the one who abandons that thirst—which is hard to abandon by the wicked-minded, which does not age as one ages,

and which is an illness that ends only with life—there is happiness.'
The cāṇḍāla said:
'Because these great lords fear from terrible fear,

as the weak fear the stronger, therefore I too am afraid.'
Paśusakha said:
'Whatever the wise, who are ever devoted to dharma, practice,

that alone is to be done by a wise man who desires the welfare of his soul.'
Having spoken thus, having cast aside those fruits containing gold,

all the sages of firm vows went elsewhere.
Then, wandering about, they came to Madhyama Puṣkara.

They saw the wandering mendicant Śunaḥsakha, who had arrived suddenly.
Having gone together with him into another part of the forest,

they saw an excellent lake, a body of water surrounded by lotuses.
Seated on the shore of the lake, meditating on the auspicious path,

Śunaḥsakha then said to all the hungry sages:
'Let all tell together: what is the pain of hunger like?'

Together they said to that wandering mendicant, Śunaḥsakha:
The sages said:
'Whatever pain is experienced when afflicted by javelins, swords, and maces,
and by discuses, lances, and arrows, even that is surpassed by hunger.

Even that caused by diseases—asthma, leprosy, consumption, internal tumours,
fever, epilepsy, and acute pain—would not be greater than hunger.

Men who are situated there, wearing bracelets of gold,
armlets, diadems, and bright earrings, do not shine when hungry.

Just as the ray of the sun draws up water that has entered the earth,
even so the channels born in the body are dried up by the digestive fire.

He does not hear, nor does he smell, nor does he see with his eye;
burned and wasted away, the deluded man is withered, afflicted by hunger.

Neither east, nor south, nor west, nor north,
nor below, nor above does one possessed by hunger perceive.

Dumbness, deafness, dullness, and lameness—
a terrifying, boundless [state] increases in hunger.

Afflicted by hunger, he abandons his father, mother, sons,
wife, daughter, brother, or kinsman.

He would not properly honour the ancestors, nor a deity, nor a guru;
and when sages have arrived, one seized by hunger does not perceive them.

In this way, these [afflictions] occur to embodied beings who are devoid of food.
Therefore, endowed with faith, one should give food in this manner;

having then become one with Brahman, he rejoices with Brahmā.
And he who gives well-prepared food day after day to a twice-born,

and who recites [this text on] the gift of food, especially at a śrāddha,
having become single-minded on the new moon day when the moon is lost,
causes it to be heard always at a śrāddha filled with the warding off of spirits.
His ancestors are satisfied for as long as he lives, without a doubt; / standing near the gods and twice-born, the giver of food is liberated.
Whether awake or heedless, or having arrived merely by chance, / or even devoid of devotion, hearing [it], he is freed from sin.
Brahmins endowed with giving are happy, sharers in dharma. / Restraint, self-control, or observance has been proclaimed by those who see the true meaning of reality.
Self-control is especially the eternal dharma of Brahmins; / self-control increases brilliance; pure self-control is supreme.
Through self-control a man becomes free from sin and radiant. / Whatever observances there are in the world, and whatever dharmas have auspicious consequences,
and the fruit of all sacrifices—self-control is superior to them; / austerity, sacrifice, and likewise giving proceed from self-control alone.
What is [the use of] the forest for the self-controlled? What indeed is the hermitage to one who is self-controlled? / Wherever the self-controlled man dwells, that is a forest, a great hermitage.
For one endowed with good conduct and virtuous behavior, whose senses are restrained, / who abides in uprightness, what need is there for hermitages?

Even in the forest faults arise for the passionate; in the home too, the restraint of the five senses is austerity. / For one who engages in blameless action, whose passion has ceased, the home is a grove of penance.

For those whose livelihood is earned by right action and dharma, who are always contented and delight in their home, / whose senses are conquered, who love guests, and who abide by observances, there is dharma even in the home.

Liberation does not belong to one devoted to grammar, nor to one devoted to attachment to caste, / nor to one intent on food and clothing, nor to one delighting in grasping the ways of worldly behavior.
For one devoted to solitude, firm in vows, turning away the pleasure of all the senses, / whose mind is absorbed in the yoga of the supreme self, who is ever harmless, liberation is certain.
The self-controlled sleeps happily and wakes up happily; / he is impartial toward all beings, whose mind is awakened.
One does not journey happily by chariot, nor by horse, nor by elephant, / as one journeys happily upon the great road by means of a disciplined self.
A lion touched, or a serpent intensely angered, / or an enemy perpetually enraged, would not do such harm as one's own self devoid of self-control.
They do not say Yama is Yama; the self indeed is called Yama. / He by whom the self is restrained (yamita) is distinguished as Yama.
"Yama, Yama," it is said; in vain the people tremble. / By whom the self is restrained, what can Yama do to him?
From flesh-eating demons and from unrestrained beings there is always danger; / for their restraint, the rod of punishment (daṇḍa) was created by the Self-born.
The rod protects beings; the rod governs the subjects; / it checks the wicked, for the rod is indeed invincible.
Dark-complexioned, youthful, red-eyed, bringing fear to all creatures, / the rod is the ruler of men, in which dharma is established.
Now, among all the stages of life, self-control alone is the supreme vow. / I shall declare those signs by which one is acclaimed as self-controlled:
freedom from stinginess, lack of harshness, contentment, proper orderliness, / absence of malice, honoring the guru, compassion toward creatures, and absence of slander.
This self-control has been declared sixfold by the sages of tranquil mind. / Dependent on compassion are dharma and liberation, and likewise heaven, O king.
He should not be angered by dishonor, nor delighted by honor; / equal in sorrow and joy, steadfast, he is proclaimed tranquil.
For the tranquil man sleeps happily, and wakes up happily; / he should abide in what is far better; the scorner perishes.
Even when insulted, he should never brood upon evil toward that person; / observing his own dharma, he should not disparage another's dharma.
He should know himself and not reprove another for faults, / whether destitute of mantras, of rituals, or even of noble birth.
Self-control covers all, like a cloth covering a deficient limb. / Those who do not understand self-control study to no purpose.
For self-control is the root of sacred learning; self-control is eternal dharma. / He who weighs self-control against gold on a balance for himself,
is celebrated as resolute because of that, and not deluded by wealth. / For all vows, self-control alone is the supreme refuge.
Even if a Brahmin knows the true meaning of the Vedas and has studied the six auxiliary limbs, / yet devoid of self-control, he does not attain venerability in this world.

The Vedas do not purify one devoid of self-control, even if studied together with the six auxiliary limbs; / Sāṃkhya and Yoga, noble family, birth, and bathings at holy places are useless.

The knower of yoga should be satisfied with dishonor as if with nectar; / and the twice-born should always shun honor as if it were poison.
From dishonor comes an increase in austerity; from honor, the decline of austerity. / Revering and honoring a Brahmin, he departs like a cow that has been milked.
Just as a cow is replenished again with grass and water, / so the twice-born is replenished again with prayers and oblations.
There is no other friend equal to a reviler in the world, / who, taking away one's bad deeds, confers his own good deeds.
He should not revile those reviling him; he should restrain his own anger. / Having restrained himself, he then sprinkles [himself] with nectar.
A begging bowl, the roots of trees, ragged garments, companionlessness, / detachment, and celibacy lead to the supreme state.
Having utterly conquered desire and anger, what will one do in the forest? / Sacred scripture is indeed maintained by practice; family is maintained by good character;
mantras are preserved by virtues; anger is mastered by purity of mind (sattva). / He who restrains anger when it has arisen in himself,
and the hero who conquers it through freedom from anger—who is equal to him on earth? / He who restrains anger when it has arisen, remaining peaceful,
him I consider the most excellent of the virtuous; that man does not sink [into sorrow]. / This is the secret, eternal heap of Brahman taught by the Grandfather,
the observance of dharma that has been extensively related by me to you. / Distinct are the worlds of sacrificers, and distinct are the worlds of ascetics;
distinct are the worlds of the self-controlled; they are indeed the most honored. / There is only one fault of the patient, and a second does not exist:
namely, that people consider one endowed with forbearance to be powerless. / But this should not be regarded as a fault; forbearance is the strength of the wise.
For him who recognizes tranquility, sacrifices and charitable works are magnified; / whatever one, filled with anger, recites, offers into fire, or worships,
all of that leaks away from him, like water from a broken pot. / He who, having risen in the morning, recites this holy chapter on self-control,
boarding the boat of dharma, will cross beyond all difficulties. / The twice-born who constantly causes this holy chapter on self-control to be heard,
attains the world of Brahmā and does not fall from there again. / Let the essence of dharma be heard, and having heard it, let it be held fast:
One should not do to others what is disagreeable to oneself; / another's wives [should be regarded] like one's mother, and another's possessions like a lump of earth;
he who looks upon all beings as himself, he truly sees. / Cooking [should be] for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva offering, and life for the sake of others;
this is the supreme essence, like gold among minerals. / Having studied that which is beneficial to all beings, O king, one attains immortality.
Having thus spoken the essence of dharma to Śunaḥsakha, / they all, accompanied by him, sat down on the bank of the lake,
looking at the extensive lake covered with water lilies and lotuses; / having descended into it, they [collected] bundles of lotus-stalks.
Having placed [their bundles of] lotus stalks on the bank of the lake, they performed the sacred water-rites; / then, emerging from that water, they gathered together,
and not seeing those lotus stalks, spoke these words: / The sages said: / "By what evil-doer, desiring food,
were the lotus stalks taken away from us who are afflicted by hunger?" / Suspicious of one another, those best of the twice-born questioned each other,
and all made a resolve, O king, to swear an oath. / Kaśyapa said: / "May he rob everything everywhere, and may he violate a trust,
and may he bear false witness, who commits the theft of the lotus stalks! / May he practice righteousness deceitfully, and may he serve a king,
and may he eat honey and meat, who commits the theft of the lotus stalks! / May he always speak untruth, and may he indulge in sensual pleasures,

and may he give his daughter for a bride-price, who commits the theft of the lotus stalks!" / Vasiṣṭha said: / "May he have intercourse outside the prescribed season, may he indulge in sleeping by day,
and may he accept mutual hospitality, who commits the theft of the lotus stalks! / A brāhmaṇa who is the husband of a Śūdra woman lives in a village with a single well;
may he attain the same world as his, who commits the theft of the lotus stalks!" / Bharadvāja said: / "May he be cruel to all, and arrogant with prosperity,
envious and slanderous, who commits the theft of the lotus stalks! / When reviled, may he revile back; when struck, may he strike another;
and may he sell juices and condiments, who commits the theft of the lotus stalks!" / Gautama said: / "Having received a guest who has arrived, may he cook separate food [for himself],
and may he always eat a Śūdra's food, who commits the theft of the lotus stalks! / After giving a gift, may he boast of it; may he take pleasure in the wife of another;
may he eat sweet food alone, who commits the theft of the lotus stalks!" / Viśvāmitra said: / "May he be ever devoted to lust, and engage in intercourse by day;
and may he always be a sinner, who commits the theft of the lotus stalks! / May he utter censure of others, and associate with others' wives,
and may he delight in slandering others, who commits the theft of the lotus stalks! / May that evil-minded one despise his mother and father;
may he hold perverse thoughts toward his mother, who commits the theft of the lotus stalks! / May he always eat food cooked by others, and consort with another's wife,
and may he become a seller of the Veda, who commits the theft of the lotus stalks!" / Jamadagni said: / "May he go into servitude to another, birth after birth,
destitute of all righteous rites, who commits the theft of the lotus stalks!" / Śunaḥsakha said: / "May he study the Vedas properly; may he be a householder fond of guests;
may he speak the truth ceaselessly, who commits the theft of the lotus stalks! / May he offer into the fire according to rule; may he perform sacrifices constantly;
may he go to the abode of Brahmā, who commits the theft of the lotus stalks!" / The sages said: / "That which was made an oath [by you] is indeed desired by the twice-born!
The theft of the lotus stalks of all of us was committed by you, O Śunaḥsakha!" / Śunaḥsakha said: / "Indeed, these lotus stalks of yours were concealed by me, O twice-born ones,
wishing to hear [discourses on] dharma; and know me to be Vāsava. / Because of your freedom from greed, imperishable worlds have been won by you, O best of sages!
Mount the aerial vehicle; let us go to the abode of the thirty [gods]!" / Then those great sages, recognizing Puraṃdara,
those skilled in speech spoke this word to Puraṃdara: / "Whatever man, having come here, enters Middle Puṣkara,
having fasted for three nights, shall obtain the necessary fruit. / That which is remembered as the twelve-year initiation of forest-dwellers—
the entire fruit of that he shall obtain here; there is no doubt. / He meets with no misfortune; he rejoices with his own attendants;
reaching the realm of Viriñci, he stays there indeed for a day of Brahmā." / Pulastya said: / Rejoicing together with Indra, they then went to heaven.
Thus, though tempted by diverse temptations here, / they did not succumb to greed at all, and so they went to heaven.

Whoever constantly hears this auspicious deed of the sages / is freed from all sins and is magnified in heaven.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, named 'The Dialogue of the Seven Sages', in the first [part], the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.

1.20.m: Bhīṣma said: / "Exceedingly wonderful and charming is this story that destroys sin! / Relate it to me in detail, truly as it happened, since I am asking.
The glorification of Middle [Puṣkara] has also been proclaimed by the sages, / and the fruit of food and the glorification of self-restraint have been related.
Tell me, O great sage, where Viṣṇu placed his step, / and how the origin of the Younger [Puṣkara] took place."
Pulastya said: / "Formerly, in the Rathaṃtara Kalpa, there was a king named Puṣpavāhana, / renowned in the worlds, equal to the sun in splendor.
Pleasured by his asceticism, the four-faced [creator], O descendant of Bharata, / gave him a golden lotus that moved at will, O king.
It wandered constantly at will through the seven continents and the world. / At the beginning of the kalpa, that continent was honored by the people who dwelt in Puṣkara,
and therefore it is called Puṣkaradvīpa. / And because that very lotus vehicle was given to him by Brahmā,
the gods and Dānavas therefore called him Puṣpavāhana. / There was no comparison here in the three worlds to that king seated on Brahmā's lotus.
Then, through the power of his asceticism, his queen, praised by thousands of women, / came to be known by name as Lāvaṇyavatī, most dear to him, just like Pārvatī to Bhava.
He had ten thousand sons, righteous of soul and foremost of archers; / beholding those sons, the king was filled with wonder again and again.

He spoke these words to the venerable Pracetas, the foremost sage who had arrived: / 'Whence has come this unshakable glory, worshipped by immortals and mortals? How was this excellent queen, resembling the lotus-born [Lakṣmī], born to me?

By the creator, pleased with my slight asceticism, this wife and this lotus-abode were given to me, O lord of sages, / into which even a hundred crores of kings entered, surrounded by ministers, elephants, chariots, and hosts of people,

and yet it is not perceived where it has gone by those who travel in the sky, and is inaccessible even to the rays of the stars, moon, and sun? / Therefore, what dharma or the like, surpassing all ordinary people, was performed [by me] born of a mother's womb,

or by all of my sons, or even by this virtuous wife? Relate all of that, O Pracetas!' / Having gazed into the previous birth, he too then said: 'Listen, O lord of the earth, to the story of the cause of that wonder!

Your birth was in a terrible hunter tribe; though born there, you were indeed a daily evil-doer. / Moreover, your body was covered on all sides with bad nails and foul-smelling creatures in the joints of your limbs.
At that time you had no friend, no son, no kinsman, no such sister, nor a mother who was blamed; / but this lovely woman, highly esteemed, most dearly beloved, and devoted, became your wife, O king.
Once upon a time, an exceedingly terrible drought occurred. For the sake of food during it, / when nothing edible such as wild fruits was obtained by you, afflicted by hunger,
a great lake rich in lotuses, its banks covered with mud, was then spotted; / taking many lotuses from there, you then went to a city named Vaidiśa.'
To obtain the price for them, you wandered through the entire city; the day was completely spent. / No buyer appeared for the lotuses, and you were utterly weary and afflicted by hunger.
Together with your wife, you sat down in the courtyard of a certain house; / then, at night, you heard there an auspicious sound.
Accompanied by your wife, you went where that auspicious sound was coming from; / there, in the middle of a sacred circle, an image of Viṣṇu was seen.
A courtesan named Anaṅgavatī, observing the dvādaśī vow, / having completed [the vow] on the twelfth day of the month of Māgha, [prepared] a mountain of salt.
She presented to her preceptor a bed furnished with all utensils, / having adorned the golden Hṛṣīkeśa with equal reverence.
She was seen by the two of them, and this thought occurred to them: / “What use are these lotuses [to us]? Better that Viṣṇu is adorned [with them].”
Thus devotion then arose in the couple, O king of men; / through that connection, having worshipped Keśava [and given] the mountain of salt,
and the bed, it was adored completely with heaps of flowers. / Then Anaṅgavatī, pleased, [ordered] three hundred measures of grain for them,
and then ordered: “Let three palas of silver be given.” / Then, relying on their noble nature, it was not accepted by the two of them.
And again, four kinds of food were brought by Anaṅgavatī for them, / and it was said: “Let the food be eaten,” O lord of the earth.
And that too was declined by the two of them: “We two will eat tomorrow, O fair-faced lady; / occasioned by you, may our fasting today bring auspiciousness.
From birth, we two are most sinful, O lady firm in vows; / occasioned by you, in your house, let there be here a small particle of merit for us.”
thus a night-wake was observed by the two through that connection; / and at dawn a bed along with a mountain of salt was given by her.
as well as a village to the preceptor with devotion, and twelve cows / accompanied by garments, ornaments, and gold to the brāhmaṇas,
along with a feast shared with friends, comrades, the poor, the blind, and the destitute. / And having honoured that hunter couple, they were dismissed.
You were that hunter born together with your wife, O lord of kings. / From that heap of lotuses and the worship of Keśava,
for you, whose sins were completely destroyed, [this became] a shrine of Puṣkara; / by the greatness of that truth, and by the austerity of non-greed, O king,
the four-faced lord of the world, pleased with you, O king of kings, / gave a vehicle moving at will. Take refuge in Puṣkara!
Having attained noble character, perform the Vibhūtidvādaśī vow / for a kalpa, O king of kings, and you will surely attain nirvāṇa.
Having spoken this, the sage vanished right there. / And the king, Puṣpavāhana, did again as was instructed.
For one who observes this, O king, there is unbroken observance of the vow. / Somehow or other over time, twelve dvādaśī [vows], O king,
are to be performed according to one's capacity, and a priestly gift given to brāhmaṇas, O king: / on the highest, cows are to be given; on the middle, excellent land;
on the lowest, gold is to be given—such is the remembered priestly gift. / The first has Brahmā as its deity, the second is dedicated to Viṣṇu,
and the third has Rudra as its deity; the three gods reside in the three. / Whoever recites or hears with devotion this [vow] which destroys the blemishes of men,
and sets his mind upon it, goes to the world of the gods and dwells there for years as numerous as the hairs [on his body]. / Now, therefore, I will proclaim the highest vow of all vows,
told by that Rudra, which destroys major sins. / Having observed the night-meal vow for a year, along with a cow to a householder,
one should give a golden discus and a trident, along with two garments, to a brāhmaṇa. / One who thus performs this merit rejoices in the world of Śiva.
This very vow is known by name as the destroyer of major sins. / But whoever subsisting on a single daily meal should present a cow accompanied by a bull,
and gives an effigy of a cow made of sesame seeds, goes to the abode of Śiva. / This is known as the Rudravrata, the destroyer of fear and sorrow.
And whoever, eating at night on alternate days, at the end of a year [gives] / a golden blue lotus along with a vessel of sugar and accompanied by a bull,
goes to the abode of Viṣṇu; this is remembered as the Nīlavrata. / For the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha, a man should abstain from oil massage;
he should give eating utensils; he goes to the dwelling of Hari. / It is called here the Prītivrata, causing love among men.
Whoever, having given up curds, milk, clarified butter, and sugarcane juice in the month of Madhu, / gives fine garments together with a vessel of liquid [sweetener],
having worshipped a brāhmaṇa couple, saying: “May Gaurī be pleased with me” / —this is called the Gaurīvrata, which grants the world of Bhavānī.
Whoever, having eaten only at night on the thirteenth day beginning with the month of Puṣya, / should then give a golden aśoka [branch] measuring ten finger-breadths along with sugarcane
to a brāhmaṇa, along with garments, saying: “May Pradyumna be pleased,” / having dwelt in the city of Viṣṇu for a kalpa, becomes free from sorrow, O king.
This is known as the Kāmavrata, constantly destroying sorrow. / Whoever, in the vow beginning in Āṣāḍha, abstains from eating fruit,
and when the four-month period has ended, on the full moon of Kārttika presents / a jar filled with clarified butter and jaggery, accompanied by gold, to a brāhmaṇa,
attains the world of Rudra; this is remembered as the Śivavrata. / Whoever abstains from flowers in the autumn and winter,
and, having fashioned three flowers of gold according to capacity on the full moon of Phālguna, / gives them at the two twilight times, saying: “May Śiva and Keśava be pleased,”
having given them, goes to the supreme abode; this is remembered as the Saumyavrata. / Whoever gives up salt on the third day of the lunar fortnight beginning with Phālguna,
gives a bed and a house furnished with utensils at the end of the year, / having worshipped a brāhmaṇa couple, saying: “May Bhavānī be pleased,”
dwells in the world of Gaurī for a kalpa; this is called the Saubhāgyavrata. / A man having observed silence during the twilights, at the end of the year presents a small jar of clarified butter,
a pair of garments, sesame seeds, and a bell to a brāhmaṇa, / goes to the world of Sarasvatī, from which return is hard to attain.
This is called the Sārasvatavrata, granting beauty and learning. / Having worshipped Lakṣmī on the fifth day, a man should fast;
at the end of the year, he should give a golden lotus accompanied by a cow. / He goes indeed to the abode of Viṣṇu, and fortune is his in birth after birth.
This is known as the Lakṣmīvrata, destroying misery and grief. / Having performed the smearing [with cow dung] before Śambhu and Keśava
for a year, a cow and a water jar are then to be given. / He becomes a king for ten thousand births; after that, he goes to the city of Śiva.
This is named the Āyurvrata, granter of all desires. / Having bowed with single-minded focus to the peepal tree, the sun, and the Gaṅgā,
a man free from envy should eat only one meal a day for one year. / At the end of the vow, a brāhmaṇa couple is to be worshipped, accompanied by three cows;
if he gives a golden tree, he obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice. / This is named the Kīrtivrata, which grants the fruit of prosperity and renown.
Having performed a bath with clarified butter for Śambhu or Keśava, / and having drawn a circle with cow dung, with unbroken grains and flowers,
at the end of the year he should give a golden lotus accompanied by a sesame cow, / and a trident measuring eight finger-breadths; he is exalted in the world of Śiva,
accompanied by the singing of Sāman chants; this is called here the Sāmavrata. / Having eaten only one meal a day on the ninth tithi, and [honouring] maidens according to capacity,
having fed [them], should give an equal [measure of gifts], a golden bodice and dress, / and should give a golden lion to a brahmin; he goes to Śiva's abode.
He will be handsome for an arbuda of births and undefeated by foes. / This is named the Vīravrata, granting happiness to men.
For four months beginning with Caitra, full of compassion, he should give water; / at the end of the vow he should give a water jar together with food and clothing,
a vessel filled with sesame seeds, and gold; he is exalted in the realm of Brahmā, / bringing about prosperity at the end of the cosmic age. This is called the Ānandavrata.
Having bathed the Lord with the five nectars for a full year, / at the end of the year he should further give a cow accompanied by the five nectars;
and he should give a conch shell to a brahmin: he attains Śiva's abode. / At the end of the cosmic age he becomes a king; this is known as the Dhṛtivrata.
A man, having abstained from meat, should give a cow at the end of the vow; / likewise, he should give a golden deer: he obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
This is called the Ahiṃsāvrata; at the end of the cosmic age he becomes an earth-ruler. / Having arisen at dawn, having bathed, he should worship a married couple,
having fed [them] according to his means with garlands, clothing, and ornaments. / He dwells in the realm of the Sun for a cosmic age; this is known as the Sūryavrata.
A man should bathe in the morning for the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha; / having given food to a brahmin, on the full moon of Kārttika he should give a cow.
He goes to the abode of Viṣṇu; this is known as the Viṣṇuvrata. / From solstice to solstice, one should avoid flowers and ghee;
at the end of that, having given flowers, food, along with a cow of ghee, / [and] rice-milk with ghee to a brahmin, he goes to Śiva's abode.
This is named the Śīlavrata, granting the fruits of good character and health. / One who undertakes the milk-vow on the fifteenth day [of each fortnight] for a full year,
performing a śrāddha at the year's end, should give five milch cows, / and yellow garments, together with jars of water.
He goes to the realm of Viṣṇu and delivers a hundred ancestors;
at the end of the cosmic age he becomes a king of kings; this is known as the Pitṛvrata. / One who offers a twilight lamp with ghee, avoiding oil,
at the year's end should give a lamp, a golden discus, and a trident, / and a pair of garments to a brahmin; that man becomes radiant,
and attains the realm of Rudra; this is known as the Dīptivrata. / On the third lunar day beginning in Kārttika, having consumed cow's urine and barley,
he should keep the night-meal vow for one year; at the year's end he should give a cow. / He dwells in the realm of Gaurī for a cosmic age; then he becomes a king here [on earth].
This is named the Rudravrata, ever bringing auspiciousness. / One who avoids fragrant ointments for four months,

1.20.m: should give a mother-of-pearl shell, fragrances, unbroken grains, and white garments to a brahmin: / he attains Varuṇa's realm; this is known as the Dṛḍhavrata.
In Vaiśākha one should avoid flowers and salt, and then, having given a cow, / dwelling in Viṣṇu's abode for a cosmic age, he becomes a king here [on earth].
This is named the Śāntivrata, granting the fruits of fame and desire. / Having fashioned a golden cosmic egg accompanied by a heap of sesame seeds,
and, giving other gifts with ghee, having satisfied the fire together with the twice-born, / having worshipped a brahmin couple with garlands, clothing, and ornaments,

according to one's means exceeding three palas, with the thought: 'May the Soul of the All be pleased,' / on an auspicious day he should give it to another brahmin; he goes to the absolute without rebirth.
This is named the Brahmavrata, granting men the fruit of nirvāṇa. / And whoever gives a cow in the act of giving birth, provided with abundant all-inclusive offerings,
and observes a milk-vow for a day, goes to the supreme abode. / This indeed is named the Suvrata, hard to obtain, free from return.
Remaining on a milk-vow for three days, [having fashioned] a golden wish-fulfilling tree, / exceeding a pala according to one's means, together with a prastha of rice,
having given it, he goes to the abode of Brahmā; this is known as the Bhīmavrata. / One who, fasting for a month, gives a splendid cow to a brahmin,
goes to the abode of Viṣṇu; this is known as the Bhīmavrata. / Having fashioned a golden earth exceeding twenty palas, one should give it;
remaining on a milk-vow for a day, he is exalted in the realm of Rudra. / This is declared as wealth-giving, enduring for seven hundred cosmic ages.
In the month of Māgha or Caitra, one should give a cow made of molasses; / performing the molasses-vow on the third lunar day, he is exalted in the realm of Gaurī.
This is named the Mahāvrata, causing supreme bliss. / One who, fasting for a fortnight, gives two brown cows to a brahmin,

attains the realm of Brahmā, well-honored by gods and asuras; / at the end of the cosmic age he becomes a sovereign over all kings; this is known as the Prabhāvrata.

Eating only one meal a day for a year, giving a water jar with edible offerings, / he dwells in Śiva's realm for a cosmic age; this is known as the Prāptivrata.

One who eats at night on the eighth lunar days, and at the end of the year gives a cow, / goes to Indra's city; it is called the Sugativrata.
One who gives firewood to a brahmin for four seasons beginning with the rains, / and at the end gives a cow made of ghee, goes to the supreme Brahman.
This is named the Vaiśvānaravrata, destroying all sins. / One who eats only at night on the eleventh lunar day and presents a discus,
having fashioned it of gold, at the end of the year attains the abode of Viṣṇu. / This is named the Kṛṣṇavrata, bestowing kingship at the end of the cosmic age.
Eating only rice-milk, at the end of the year he should give a pair of cows to a brahmin; / he dwells in Lakṣmī's realm for a cosmic age; this is known as the Devīvrata.
Eating only at night on the seventh lunar day, at the conclusion he should give a milch cow: / he attains the realm of the Sun; this is known as the Bhānuvrata.
Eating at night on the fourth lunar day, at the end he should likewise give gold and a pair of cows; / this is named the Vaināyaka, granting the fruit of Śiva's realm.

One who, having renounced great fruits during the four months of the rainy season, gives golden ones / to a twice-born man in Kārttika, and likewise a pair of cows at the conclusion of the fire offering—
this is named the Sauravrata, granting the fruit of the realm of the Sun. / O king, one who completes twelve twelfth lunar days by fasting,
a man should worship brahmins according to his means with cows, clothing, and gold: / he attains the supreme abode; this is known as the Viṣṇuvrata.
Eating at night on the fourteenth lunar day, giving a pair of cows at the end of the year, / he attains Śiva's abode; this is known as the Traiyambaka.
Having fasted for seven nights, he should give a jar of ghee to a twice-born man; / they call this the Varavrata, granting the fruit of Brahmā's realm.
Reaching Kāśī, he gives a milch cow: / he dwells in Indra's realm for a cosmic age; this is known as the Mantravrata.
Renouncing mouth-fresheners, at the end of the year he should give a cow; / he attains Varuṇa's realm; it is called the Vāruṇavrata.
And one who performs the cāndrāyaṇa penance should offer a golden moon; / this is declared as the Candravrata, granting the fruit of the Moon's realm.
In Jyeṣṭha, at the end of [the penance of] the five fires, giving a golden cow / on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, he goes to heaven; this is known as the Rudravrata.
Once he should perform the ritual in Śiva's abode on the third lunar day; / at its completion, giving a cow, he goes [to heaven]; it is called the Bhavānīvrata.
In Māgha, he should have wet garments at night, and on the seventh lunar day give a cow; / having dwelt in heaven for a cosmic age, he becomes a king here [on earth]; this is the Pavanavrata.
Having fasted for three nights, on the full moon of Phālguna he should give a fair dwelling: / he attains the realm of Āditya; this is known as the Dhāmavrata.
Fasting, worshipping a married couple at the three twilights with ornaments, / giving [gifts], he attains liberation; this is known as the Mokṣavrata.
Having given a vessel of salt on the bright second lunar day to the Moon, / one who gives a cow to a Brahmin upon its completion goes to the abode of Śiva.
Likewise, O king of kings, [having given] bell-metal with a garment, accompanied by a priestly fee, / and he who gives a cow upon its completion goes to the abode of Śiva.
At the end of a kalpa he becomes a king of kings; this is handed down as the vow to Soma. / Eating once a day on the first lunar days, and giving fruit upon its completion,
he goes to the station of Vaiśvānara; this is handed down as the vow to Fire. / [Giving] a golden chariot weighing more than two palas, joined with a pair of horses,
having observed a fast, one who gives [it] would dwell in heaven for a hundred kalpas; / at the end of that, he would become a king of kings. This is handed down as the vow of the horse.
Likewise, he should give a golden chariot joined with two elephants; / the ruler of the earth would dwell in the world of truth even for a thousand kalpas.
Having returned here, he would become [a king] on earth; this is handed down as the vow of the elephant. / Eating once a day on the tenth lunar day, giving ten milch cows upon its completion,
and giving a golden lamp, he becomes sovereign of the universe. / This is the vow named Viśva, which destroys great sins.
Moreover, he who will perform the gift of a maiden at Puṣkara on the full-moon day of Kārttika, / endowed with twenty-one virtues, will go to the world of Brahmā.
There is no gift greater than the gift of a maiden, nowhere more excellent; / particularly so at Puṣkara, and most especially on the full-moon day of Kārttika.
It should be given to a Brahmin according to rule; their world shall be imperishable. / Having made an elephant composed of sesame-flour, accompanied by jewels,
those men who present it to a Brahmin while standing in the midst of water, / theirs indeed shall be an imperishable world until the dissolution of beings.
He who reads or even hears this unexcelled group of sixty vows, / he too would become the sovereign of Gandharvas for a hundred manvantaras.

This holy group of sixty vows, beneficial to all humanity, has been told to you today, O descendant of Bharata. / If there is a desire in you to hear, O king of kings, hear this which is to be performed by a twice-born:
There is no purity or purification of mind without bathing; / therefore, for the purification of the mind, bathing is prescribed at the beginning.
One should perform the bath with uncollected or collected waters; / the wise one, knowing the mantras, should consecrate the sacred waters with the root mantra.
‘Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa’ is proclaimed to be the root mantra. / With darbha-grass in hand, having sipped water according to rule, restrained, and clean,
having measured out a square of four cubits on all sides, / the discerning one should invoke the Gaṅgā with these mantras:
‘You are born from the foot of Viṣṇu, Vaiṣṇavī, with Viṣṇu as your deity; / save us from sin from birth to the end in death!
Vāyu said that there are three and a half crores of sacred waters / in heaven, on earth, and in the atmosphere; they are in you, O Jāhnavī!
Nandinī indeed is your name, and Nalinī among the gods, / Dakṣā, Pṛthvī, Subhagā, Viśvakāyā, Śivā, Sitā,
Vidyādharī, Suprasannā, likewise Lokaprasādinī, / Kṣemā, and Jāhnavī, Śāntā, and Śāntipradāyinī.’
One should recite these holy names at the time of bathing; / the Gaṅgā that goes through the three paths will become present there.
With the cavity of the hands filled with water, consecrated by reciting seven times, / he should pour water over his head three, four, five, or seven times again.
He should likewise take a bath with clay, having addressed it according to the rule: / ‘O earth traversed by the horse, traversed by the chariot, traversed by Viṣṇu,
O clay, take away my sin, whatever misdeed has been done by me! / You were lifted up by the boar, by hundred-armed Kṛṣṇa.
Obeisance to you, the source and kindling-stick of all worlds, O you of noble vows!’ / Having bathed thus, one should then properly sip water according to rule.
Arising and putting on two clean, pure garments, / one should then perform the libation for the satiation of the three worlds.
One should first offer libations to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the Prajāpatis, / gods, yakṣas, and nāgas, hosts of gandharvas and apsarases,
cruel serpents and birds, trees, Jambhakas and others, / vidyādharas, clouds, and likewise beings that move in the sky,
and whichever living beings have no support, and whichever delight in sinful conduct: / ‘This water is offered by me for the satiation of them.’
Having worn the sacred thread over the left shoulder for the gods, one should then wear it around the neck; / with devotion one should offer libations to humans, sons of sages, and sages:
Sanaka, Sananda, and thirdly Sanātana, / Kapila, Āsuri, Voḍhu, and Pañcaśikha:
‘May all of them always attain satisfaction by the water given by me.’ / To Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and also Nārada, / to all divine sages and celestial sages one should offer libations with water and unbroken grains.
Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder, and placing the right knee upon the ground, / to the Agniṣvāttas, the Saumyas, the Haviṣmants, the Uṣmapās,
the Sukālins, the Barhiṣads, and again the Ājyapās, / one should satisfy the ancestors with devotion, with water mixed with sesame and sandal paste.
With darbha-grass in hand, according to rule, one should then satisfy one’s own ancestors, / the father and others by name and gotra, and likewise maternal grandfathers.
Having offered libations according to rule with devotion, he should utter this mantra: / ‘Those who are kin, those who are not kin, and those who were kin in another birth,
may all of them attain satisfaction, and whoever desires water from us.’ / Having properly sipped water according to rule, he should draw a lotus in front.
With water containing unbroken grains, with flowers, with sesame and red sandal, / he should carefully offer the arghya with recitation of the names of the Sun:
‘Obeisance to you whose form is the universe, obeisance to you who have the form of Viṣṇu! / O you who are bowed to by all the gods, be pleased with me, O maker of light!
Obeisance to you, maker of the day! Obeisance to you, maker of radiance!’ / Having thus bowed down to the Sun, and having circumambulated him three times,
seeing and touching a twice-born, a cow, and gold, he should go home. / Then he should worship the holy image situated in his own house;

And thereafter he should arrange for feeding, beginning with the twice-born. / By this rule all the sages attained perfection.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, named ‘The Rule of Bathing’, in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
